summary: Defines how MPLS label switching can run over Frame Relay networks, including the model and generic mechanisms used. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Frame Relay is an older kind of network. This explains how to run the tag-based MPLS forwarding system on top of it.

questions: how does mpls work over frame relay
how is the dlci used as an mpls label
how is ttl handled on frame relay lsps
subtitle: How a Frame Relay switch can act as an MPLS label switching router by carrying labels in the DLCI field.

tldr.problem: Existing Frame Relay switches forward by DLCI and cannot decrement an IP-style TTL, yet operators could reuse them as MPLS label switching routers if the labels fit Frame Relay's rules.
tldr.mechanism: The top MPLS label travels in the DLCI field of the Frame Relay header while the rest of the generic MPLS encapsulation rides behind it. Labels are handed out with LDP using downstream-on-demand allocation, and TTL is adjusted at the edges of the Frame Relay segment.
tldr.outcome: Frame Relay switches can join an MPLS network as FR-LSRs, alongside other link types. It is a Proposed Standard companion to the MPLS label stack and ATM documents.

facts.label: Default hop count
facts.value: 1 when LDP gives none or unknown

today: RFC 3034 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It was written alongside RFC 3032 (label stack encoding) and RFC 3035 (the ATM counterpart).

sections.title: Frame Relay Switches as Label Switching Routers
sections.content:
RFC 3034 explains how Frame Relay switches can serve as Label Switching Routers (LSRs) in the Multiprotocol Label Switching architecture described in RFC 3031. Such switches run network layer routing (the RFC names OSPF and IS-IS) and forward based on the results. No specific Frame Relay routing is needed.

The top (current) label, the one forwarding decisions use, is carried in the DLCI field of the Frame Relay data link header. Any other information that travels with the label, and any further labels in a stack, ride in the generic MPLS encapsulation defined in RFC 3032. Permanent virtual circuits (PVCs) can be configured to carry this label-switched traffic. The document is a companion to RFC 3032 and RFC 3035 (the ATM equivalent).
sections.plainLanguage: An old network of switches that route by a circuit number can be reused for tag-based forwarding. The circuit number simply becomes the tag.

sections.title: What Makes Frame Relay Switches Special
sections.content:
A Frame Relay switch is limited by its (possibly pre-existing) hardware and by the Frame Relay standards, so an FR-LSR needs special procedures. The RFC lists the features that matter:

  • Label swapping happens on the DLCI field in the frame header, which sets the size and place of the label. The DLCI can be 10 bits (the default) or 23 bits, spanning two or four bytes.
  • There is generally no way to perform an IP-style TTL decrement.
  • Each node does congestion control from parameters passed at circuit creation, and may set flags in frame headers when congestion occurs or the circuit's contract is exceeded.
  • Several input DLCIs can often be merged onto one output DLCI (multipoint-to-point), but multipoint-to-multipoint circuits are generally not fully supported.

The RFC also defines its own vocabulary: an LC-FR interface is a Frame Relay interface under label switching control, an FR-LSR forwards frames between two such interfaces using the DLCI, and an FR-LSR domain is a set of FR-LSRs joined by LC-FR interfaces. The Edge Set is the set of LSRs attached to the domain by LC-FR interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Old switches are a bit simple. They only know how to swap the circuit number and cannot count hops like a router does, so the rules have to work around that.

sections.title: Label Encapsulation
sections.content:
By default, labeled packets are sent with the generic label encapsulation of RFC 3032, using the Frame Relay null encapsulation. The frame begins with a Q.922 address of length n, which is 2 or 4 octets, followed by the MPLS packet. The DLCI is written into that Q.922 address, in the 10-bit or the 23-bit layout.

Because of null encapsulation, labels implicitly encode the network protocol type. The generic encapsulation holds one entry per label in the stack. The top entry carries meaningful EXP, S and TTL values, but its label value lives in the DLCI field instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag goes in the spot on the envelope where the circuit number normally sits. The rest of the MPLS information follows inside.

sections.title: Processing at Ingress, Core and Egress
sections.content:
Both ends of a link need a full-duplex connection for LDP, and the DLCI for that LDP circuit is set by configuration. Apart from that, the DLCI values used for MPLS in the two directions are treated as independent spaces. The allowed DLCI ranges, DLCI size and support for VC merging must be communicated through LDP messages.

An ingress FR-LSR forwards the packet by normal network layer rules, then puts at least one label entry on it. The TTL in the top entry is filled from the network layer TTL, and the top label becomes the output DLCI. A core FR-LSR behaves like a conventional Frame Relay switch: it looks the arriving DLCI up in its DLCI Information Base, swaps it for the outgoing DLCI and transmits. At the egress, the label stack is popped. The stack carries no explicit network protocol field, so the protocol is inferred from the value of the label that was popped.

LSPs may be homogeneous (the same stack encoding on every hop) or heterogeneous. In a heterogeneous LSP an LSR may swap off a Frame Relay encoded label and put a label in a generic MPLS (shim) header on the next hop. FR-LSRs SHOULD operate on loop-free paths, SHOULD use loop detection and MAY use loop prevention.
sections.plainLanguage: The first switch attaches a tag. Middle switches just swap the old tag for the next one. The last switch takes the tag off and delivers the message.

sections.title: TTL Handling Across a Frame Relay Segment
sections.content:
Frame Relay switches do not decrement TTL, so a run of FR-LSRs forms a non-TTL segment. A packet leaving it should still show the number of LSR hops it crossed. The RFC expresses this as output TTL = input TTL - d, where d is 0, 1 or the number of hops of the LSP segment, depending on the input, forwarding and output encapsulations.

For unicast packets, the ingress FR-LSR SHOULD decrement the MPLS TTL by the number of hops of the Frame Relay segment. The hop count comes from LDP; if LDP gave none, or an unknown value, the default is 1. When a binding is passed upstream the hop count is incremented by 1 (unknown stays unknown). If it would exceed the maximum, the FR-LSR MUST NOT pass the binding upstream and MUST send an error instead.

If the TTL would expire before the packet reaches the end of the segment, the ingress MUST NOT label switch it. It follows RFC 3032: treat the packet as expired and return an ICMP message, or forward it unlabeled with a TTL reflecting IP forwarding. If the incoming TTL is 1, only the first option applies. For multicast, the ingress decrements by 1 and the egress is the node that accounts for the segment length.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal routers count hops by taking one off a counter each time. These switches cannot, so the first or last one subtracts the whole trip in one go.

sections.title: Control Component and Label Allocation
sections.content:
A Frame Relay switch used for label switching MUST implement the label switching control component, and it MUST take part as a peer in network layer routing protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS. Label bindings MAY be distributed by several mechanisms, one being the Label Distribution Protocol (RFC 3036). Conformance is required only to the Frame Relay Forum UNI agreement (framing, bit-stuffing, headers, FCS), except its PVC signaling (LMI). Q.933 signaling is not required. If no circuit parameters are given, the default should be zero CIR, so policing sets the DE bit but no frames are dropped. The label switching and standard Frame Relay control components can coexist on one switch as a hybrid, where they run independently.

Labels are allocated with downstream-on-demand, which MUST be used by FR-LSRs that do not support VC merging. An edge LSR sends an LDP request for a route to its next hop and stores the label from the mapping reply. A FR-LSR that receives a request allocates a label and passes the request downstream. In ordered control it waits for the downstream mapping before replying upstream; in independent control it replies at once with an unknown hop count and corrects it later. When the next hop changes, the old one gets an LDP release; when a request cannot be satisfied, the requester is told with a withdraw. If the LDP session is lost, the LSR MUST discard bindings learned through it.

Label space can be saved by merging: one label serves several routes, so an LSR that already has an outgoing binding for a FEC need not request another. Merging is restricted when frames are fragmented, because fragments of different frames must not be interleaved.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, switches ask the next switch down the line for a tag, and each one passes the question along until the end answers. Then the tags are handed back up the line.

sections.title: Frame Relay Fields in LDP Messages
sections.content:
LDP messages between Frame Relay peers can carry three Frame Relay specific items. The Frame Relay Label Range gives a Minimum DLCI and a Maximum DLCI, each a 23-bit value right justified, that bound the block of DLCIs the sender supports. The Frame Relay Merge item is a single bit: 0 means merge is not supported, 1 means it is. A FR-LSR that supports VC merging MUST ensure fragmented frames from different incoming DLCIs are not interleaved on the outgoing DLCI. The Frame Relay Label carries the DLCI itself.

Both the range and the label include a 2-bit Len field saying how many bits the DLCI has. Reserved fields are set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: When two switches talk, they tell each other which range of circuit numbers they can use and whether they can combine streams.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC looks at security for frame traffic and for label distribution. MPLS encapsulation has no effect on authenticated or encrypted network layer packets: IP packets that are authenticated or encrypted incur no change.

MPLS itself has no mechanism to protect against misdirection of packets, or against an LSR being impersonated by accident or on purpose. Altering a label in the DLCI field, or fields in a label stack that follows, changes how the frame is forwarded. The label distribution mechanism can be secured by applying authentication or encryption to the underlying protocol that carries label information, as described in RFC 3036.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone changes the tag on a message, it goes to the wrong place. The tag system has no lock of its own, so the messages that hand out tags need their own protection.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Len
fields.desc: Number of DLCI bits: 0 means 10 bits, 2 means 23 bits.

fields.name: DLCI
fields.desc: Binary value of the label, using 10 or 23 significant bits.

messages.label: LDP request
messages.note: Asks for a label binding for a route (FEC).

messages.label: LDP request
messages.note: Allocates a label, then passes the request downstream.

messages.label: LDP mapping
messages.note: Returns a label with the hop count object set to 1.

messages.label: LDP mapping
messages.note: Hop count incremented by 1 before it goes upstream.
